Lock picking is essentially the art of manipulating a lock’s internal components—usually pins and springs—without using a key. It’s a bit like a puzzle where the goal is to align the pins so the lock’s mechanism can turn.

Most locks have a series of pins held in place by springs. When you insert a key, it lifts these pins to a specific height, allowing the plug to rotate. A hobbyist uses a tension wrench to apply a slight rotational force to the plug while using a pick to lift the pins one by one. If you get the tension and the lift just right, the pins will settle into the "shear line," and the plug will turn.

It’s a skill that requires a lot of patience and a steady hand. You’re essentially listening and feeling for the subtle resistance of the pins as you work. It’s less about force and more about understanding how the lock is built and how its parts interact.
